standard_text: Demonstrate which values from a specified set, if any, make the equation or inequality true. Use substitution to determine whether a given number in a specified set makes an equation or inequality true.

skills.name: Substitute a value for a variable and check whether the statement is true

prerequisite_skill.description: Read =, <, and > as a question (Are the two sides equal? Is the left smaller? Is the left bigger?) and replace a letter in a number sentence with a given value.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: If x = 3, what number do you write in place of x in the sentence x + 4 = 7? Is the sentence true?

skills.i_do_script: Today we're testing whether a given number makes a number sentence true. Don't tell the student the rule first — ask what the equal sign is asking, and let them discover that both sides have to match. Listen for students who only compute one side and forget to compare back.

canonical_error.pattern: Student computes the side with the variable but never checks it against the other side, or treats the equal sign as 'and then write the answer' rather than as a true/false question.
canonical_error.example: Given x + 4 = 7 and asked whether x = 5 makes it true, the student writes 5 + 4 = 9 and circles 'yes' because they got an answer, not noticing 9 does not equal 7.
canonical_error.why: The student is still using = the way they did in early arithmetic — as a 'compute now' signal — instead of as a relation that the two sides must satisfy. They never compare back to the right side.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on — let's check both sides.
redirect_script.prompt: Cover the letter, write the value in its place, then circle the sign in the middle and ask out loud, 'Is the left side really equal to (or less than, or greater than) the right side?'
redirect_script.praise: Nice — you tested both sides before deciding.

vocabulary.definition: A number sentence that says two things are equal, using the = sign.
A number sentence that uses <, >, less-than-or-equal, or greater-than-or-equal to compare two things.
The specific number you put in place of the variable.
The sentence is correct after you substitute — both sides match the comparison.

next_steps.if_fail: Re-teach what =, <, and > are asking before moving on.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 'x + 4 = 7. Does x = 3 make this true?'
Read this with me. What do you think the letter x is doing in this sentence?
The problem tells us x = 3. If x is just standing in for the number 3, what would we write in place of x in the sentence?
Watch for the student to write 3 + 4 = 7. If they freeze on the letter, prompt: 'Cover the x with your finger and write 3 there instead.'
Look at the equal sign in the middle. What is the equal sign asking us — is it telling us to compute, or is it asking a question about the two sides?
Now compute the left side. What does 3 + 4 give you? And what is on the right side?
So is the left side really equal to the right side? Yes or no — and how do you know?
Try this one: same sentence x + 4 = 7, but now someone says x = 5. Walk me through it the same way — substitute, compute, then compare. Is it true or false?

skills.name: Pick which whole-number value from a list makes a one-step equation true
skills.i_do_script: When you see a question that gives you an equation and a list of numbers to choose from, the smart move is to test each number, not guess the one that 'looks right.' We're going to walk through one together, and I want you to do the thinking out loud — I'll just ask the questions. Your only job is to make sure both sides of the equation match after you swap the letter for a number.

canonical_error.pattern: Student picks the value that 'looks related' to the numbers in the equation instead of substituting each candidate and checking, often grabbing the right-side number itself or the difference of the two visible numbers.
canonical_error.example: For x + 6 = 14 with choices 6, 7, 8, 9, the student picks 6 because 6 appears in the equation, or picks 14 if it is offered, instead of substituting each choice and computing.
canonical_error.why: The student sees numbers in the equation and reaches for a surface-level match instead of treating each choice as a hypothesis to test. They have not internalized the substitute-and-check loop as the actual procedure for these items.

redirect_script.stop: Stop — you picked a number, but you didn't test it. We have to put it in and see if both sides match.
redirect_script.prompt: Point at choice A. Write the equation with that number in place of the variable. Compute the left side. Is it equal to the right side? Yes or no? Now do the same for B, C, and D. Whichever one makes both sides match is the answer.
redirect_script.praise: You substituted every choice and only picked the one where both sides were equal. That's the whole job.

The value that makes the equation true. When you substitute it in, both sides match.

worked_example_script.text: Let's look at this one together: 'Which value of x makes the equation x + 5 = 12 true?' The four choices are 7, 5, 12, and 17.
What is the equal sign asking us in this problem? When we plug a number in for x, what has to be true about the left side and the right side?
Let's start with the first choice, 7. If x = 7, what does the left side of the equation become? Read it out loud: 7 plus 5 equals what?
You got 12 on the left side. The right side is also 12. So when x = 7, do both sides match? Is the equation true?
Before we lock it in, let's make sure the other choices don't also work. If we tried x = 5, the left side would be 5 + 5. What do you get? Does that equal 12?
What about x = 12? Plug it in: 12 + 5 equals what? Is that 12?
And x = 17? 17 + 5 equals what? Is that 12?
So out of all four choices, which one was the only number that made both sides match? And what did we have to do to every choice to be sure?

practice_problems.stem: If x = 6, is the equation x + 3 = 9 true?
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- substitute: 6 + 3 = 9, and both sides match.

practice_problems.stem: Which value makes x + 2 = 9 true: 7 or 11?
practice_problems.answer: 7 -- test it: 7 + 2 = 9. Testing 11 gives 13, which is not 9.

practice_problems.stem: Which value of x makes x + 8 = 15 true? Choices: 7, 8, 15, 23.
practice_problems.answer: 7 -- 7 + 8 = 15. The choices 8 and 15 are just numbers copied from the equation, and 23 comes from adding 8 + 15.
practice_problems.notes: The wrong choices are all 'number grabs' -- watch who tests versus who matches.

practice_problems.stem: Which value of n makes 5n = 35 true? Choices: 7, 30, 40, 175.
practice_problems.answer: 7 -- 5 x 7 = 35. The other choices come from subtracting, adding, or multiplying the two visible numbers instead of testing.
practice_problems.notes: 5n means 5 times n -- some students will read it as the digits 5 and n side by side.

practice_problems.stem: Marcus answered this problem: 'Which value of x makes x + 6 = 14 true? Choices: 6, 8, 14, 20.' Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Marcus: '14 is right there in the equation, so that has to be it.'
practice_problems.answer: Marcus grabbed a number he saw instead of testing. Substitute 14: 14 + 6 = 20, not 14 -- false. Test 8: 8 + 6 = 14 -- true. The answer is x = 8.
practice_problems.notes: Direct bait for the canonical 'picks the number that looks related' error.

practice_problems.stem: Which value of y makes y - 9 = 6 true? Choices: 3, 6, 9, 15.
practice_problems.answer: 15 -- 15 - 9 = 6. Students who compute 9 - 6 grab 3; students who copy grab 6 or 9.

practice_problems.stem: Write your own equation whose solution is x = 5, then prove it by substituting.
practice_problems.answer: Any correct equation, e.g. x + 4 = 9 (check: 5 + 4 = 9) or 3x = 15 (check: 3 x 5 = 15).
practice_problems.notes: Producing an equation shows the student owns the relationship, not just the checking routine.

practice_problems.stem: Which value makes x / 3 = 4 true: 7, 12, or 15? Test each one, then mark the solution on the number line.
practice_problems.answer: 12 -- 12 / 3 = 4. (7 / 3 is not a whole number, and 15 / 3 = 5.) Mark the point at 12.
practice_problems.notes: Placing the answer forces the student to hold its size, not just circle a letter.

activities.title: Does 6 Make It True?
materials: Equation cards (cut apart)
Two header cards: TRUE when n = 6 / FALSE when n = 6
activities.instructions:
1. Lay the two headers on the desk. The test value is n = 6 for every card.
2. Partners take turns drawing a card, substituting 6 out loud, and placing it under TRUE or FALSE.
3. The partner must agree or challenge before the next draw -- a challenge means both write the substitution out.
4. Debrief: which card almost fooled you, and what saved you?

activities.title: The Number-Grabber
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show the group Marcus's work and let them talk before you do.
2. Ask: why did 14 look so tempting? (His instinct is sensible -- 14 IS in the problem.)
3. Have the group run the actual test on 14 and on 8, writing both substitutions.
4. Each student writes Marcus a one-sentence tip that starts with 'Before you pick...'

content.worked_problem: Which value of x makes x + 6 = 14 true? Choices: 6, 8, 14, 20. Marcus picked 14.
content.error_step: Marcus matched a number he could see in the equation instead of substituting each choice and checking.
content.why: Substituting 14 gives 14 + 6 = 20, which is not 14 -- so 14 fails its own test. Only testing reveals that 8 + 6 = 14 is true. The visible numbers in an equation are almost never the solution.

activities.title: Test It or Toss It
materials: Mini whiteboards
A list of equations with one candidate value each
activities.instructions:
1. Write an equation and one candidate value on the board, e.g. 'x + 7 = 12, try x = 5.'
2. Every student substitutes, computes, and writes TEST PASSED or TOSS IT with the check shown (5 + 7 = 12).
3. On 'show,' all boards go up at once.
4. Pick one student to read their check out loud: substitute, compute, compare.
5. Debrief after 6-8 rounds: what did you do before deciding, every single time?

strategy_links.why: The substitute-compute-compare loop is a routine to model, share, and hand over -- exactly the gradual-release arc.
Whiteboard Pass makes every student's test visible, so number-grabbing can't hide behind a circled letter.
Analyzing a number-grab like Marcus's makes the 'looks related' trap explicit and gives students language to catch it.

questioning_prompts: Before you pick, how will you TEST that number?
What does the equal sign ask about the two sides after you substitute?
You tried x = 5 -- what did the left side become, and what did it need to be?
Could two of these choices both work? How would you find out for sure?
Which choice did you cross off fastest, and what told you to?

misconception_redirects.praise: You substituted every choice and only picked the one where both sides were equal. That's the whole job.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student substitutes and computes correctly but then reports the TOTAL as the answer -- '8 + 6 is 14, so the answer is 14.'
misconception_redirects.say: The answer is the number we put IN for the letter, not the total we got out. Which number did you write in place of x? Circle it -- that's your solution.
misconception_redirects.praise: Right -- the solution is the value that went in, and your check proves it works.

8, with the check '2 x 8 = 16' stated. Picking 14 signals grabbing the biggest visible number instead of testing.

skills.name: Determine which value from a list makes a one-step equation true

prerequisite_skill.description: Substitute a value into a one-step equation and verify whether both sides are equal.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Does x = 6.2 make the equation 2.45x = 15.19 true? Show how you checked.

skills.i_do_script: On these problems you get one equation and four candidate values, and your job is to find the value that makes both sides match. With decimals, eyeballing won't cut it -- you have to substitute each candidate and actually compute. We'll walk through one together by asking ourselves the same question for every choice: does the left side land exactly on the right side?

canonical_error.pattern: Student stops at the first value that 'looks close' to the right side instead of substituting carefully, especially when decimals are involved.
canonical_error.example: For 2.45x = 15.19, the student picks x = 6.11 because 2.45 times 6 is roughly 14.7 and 6.11 is the middle choice, instead of computing 2.45 times 6.11 (about 14.97) and rejecting it.
canonical_error.why: The student is estimating rather than substituting. They never actually multiply each candidate, so they cannot check the equality precisely — the decimal precision is exactly what the spec is testing.

redirect_script.prompt: Pick one choice, write the multiplication out on paper, and compare your result to the right side. If it doesn't match exactly, cross that choice off.
redirect_script.praise: Good — you tested each value instead of guessing.

vocabulary.definition: A statement that two expressions are equal.
A value of the variable that makes the equation true.
Replace the variable with the value you are testing.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 3x = 12. Does x = 4 make it true?
Look at the equal sign in the middle. Is it telling us to compute, or is it asking a question -- do the two sides match?
The problem hands us x = 4. What does 3x mean, and if x is 4, what do we write in place of 3x on the left side?
Now multiply it out: what is 3 times 4? And what number is sitting on the right side?

Watch here: a student may just glance at the 3, the 4, and the 12 and say 'yes, looks right' without ever multiplying. Stop them: 'Did you actually multiply? 3 times 4 has to land exactly on 12, not just look close.'
So the left side came out to 12 and the right side is 12. Are they exactly equal -- true or false?
Say it as our final answer: does x = 4 make 3x = 12 true, and how do we know?

practice_problems.stem: Does x = 4 make the equation 3x = 12 true?
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- 3 x 4 = 12, and both sides match exactly.

practice_problems.stem: Does n = 2.5 make the equation n + 1.5 = 4 true?
Which value of x makes 1.5x = 4.5 true? Choices: 3, 3.5, 4.5, 6.
practice_problems.answer: 3 -- 1.5 x 3 = 4.5 exactly. (1.5 x 3.5 = 5.25; 4.5 is the right side copied; 6 comes from adding 1.5 + 4.5.)

practice_problems.stem: Which value of y makes y + 2.7 = 8.2 true? Choices: 5.5, 5.9, 6.5, 10.9.
practice_problems.answer: 5.5 -- 5.5 + 2.7 = 8.2 exactly. 10.9 comes from adding the two visible numbers; 5.9 and 6.5 are 'close' traps.
practice_problems.notes: All three wrong answers survive estimation -- only exact addition kills them.

practice_problems.stem: Dana solved this one by estimating. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Dana: '2.6 times 3 is about 7.8, so the answer is just a little more than 3. I'll take 3.1.'
practice_problems.answer: Dana estimated instead of substituting. Actually multiply: 2.6 x 3.1 = 8.06 -- not 8.32, so 3.1 fails. Test 3.2: 2.6 x 3.2 = 8.32 -- true. The answer is x = 3.2.
practice_problems.notes: Bait for the canonical 'looks close' error -- estimation picks the wrong neighbor.

practice_problems.stem: Which value of n makes n + 0.75 = 2 true? Choices: 1.25, 1.35, 2.75.
practice_problems.answer: 1.25 -- 1.25 + 0.75 = 2.00 exactly. (1.35 gives 2.10; 2.75 comes from adding the visible numbers.)

practice_problems.stem: Which value makes 0.5x = 3 true: 1.5, 6, or 6.5? Test each candidate, then mark the solution on the number line.
practice_problems.notes: Multiplying by 0.5 makes numbers smaller -- placing 6 on the line surfaces students who expected the solution to be less than 3.

practice_problems.stem: Make up a decimal equation whose solution is x = 2.5, then prove it with substitution.
practice_problems.answer: Any correct equation, e.g. 2x = 5 (check: 2 x 2.5 = 5) or x + 1.5 = 4 (check: 2.5 + 1.5 = 4).
practice_problems.notes: Producing the equation reverses the direction -- recognition isn't ownership.

activities.title: Match the Equation to Its Solution
materials: Equation cards and solution cards (cut apart)
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the equation cards on the left and the solution cards on the right.
2. Partners take turns claiming a match -- but a claim only counts if you say the substitution out loud: 'two point five times four is ten.'
3. Two solution cards match nothing; if you end up holding one, a check somewhere went wrong -- find it together.
4. Debrief: which pair could NOT be matched by estimating alone?

activities.title: Dana's Shortcut
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show Dana's estimate-only work and let the group react first.
2. Ask: what was smart about Dana's thinking? (Estimation DID narrow the field -- it just can't finish the job.)
3. Have the group compute 2.6 x 3.1 and 2.6 x 3.2 by hand and see where the estimate lied.
4. Each student writes one sentence: 'Estimation is for ___, substitution is for ___.'

content.worked_problem: 2.6x = 8.32 with choices 3.1, 3.2, 3.6. Dana estimated 2.6 x 3 as 'about 7.8' and picked 3.1.
content.error_step: Dana stopped at the estimate and picked the nearest-looking choice instead of multiplying each candidate exactly.
content.why: When the choices differ by a tenth, estimation cannot tell them apart: 2.6 x 3.1 = 8.06 and 2.6 x 3.2 = 8.32. Only exact multiplication reveals which one lands on 8.32.

activities.title: Exact or Out
materials: Mini whiteboards
activities.instructions:
1. Post a decimal equation with ONE candidate value, e.g. '2.4x = 7.44, try x = 3.'
2. Students must write the full computation (2.4 x 3 = 7.20), then EXACT if it lands on the right side or OUT if it misses -- even by a penny.
3. Boards up together. Anyone who wrote 'close enough' owes the class the exact product.
4. After 6 rounds, ask: why is 'about right' never good enough for an equation?

strategy_links.why: Thinking aloud through one full exact check -- substitute, multiply carefully, compare -- models the precision that separates this skill from estimating.
Short number talks on decimal products (what is 2.4 x 3.1, and how do you know?) build the computation confidence the checks depend on.
Pairing a correct worked check with Dana's estimate-only work makes the contrast between 'close' and 'equal' the explicit lesson.

questioning_prompts: Is 'close' good enough for an equation? What does the equal sign demand?
What did you get when you actually multiplied -- not estimated?
Which choices can you eliminate with an estimate, and which two need the exact product to tell apart?
Where will the decimal point land in your product? How do you know before you multiply?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student stops at the first value that 'looks close' to the right side instead of substituting carefully, especially with decimals.
misconception_redirects.say: Pick one choice, write the multiplication out on paper, and compare your result to the right side. If it doesn't match exactly, cross that choice off.
misconception_redirects.praise: Good — you tested each value instead of guessing.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student multiplies decimals but places the decimal point wrong, getting an answer ten times too big or too small.
misconception_redirects.say: Count the decimal digits in both factors -- your product needs that many decimal places. Multiply as whole numbers first, then place the point last.
misconception_redirects.praise: Nice -- you placed the decimal point deliberately instead of hoping.

quick_checks.look_for: Yes, with '2.5 x 4 = 10' stated. A shrug or 'looks about right' means the student is estimating, not substituting.

quick_checks.prompt: 2.45 x 6 = 14.70. So is x = 6 a solution to 2.45x = 15.19?
quick_checks.look_for: No -- 14.70 is not 15.19. A yes means 'close enough' thinking, the exact error this skill exists to kill.

sentence_starters: I computed exactly and got ___, which does / does not equal ___.
I crossed off ___ because the left side came out to ___, not ___.

worked_solution.stem: Which value of x makes 2.4x = 7.44 true? Choices: 3, 3.1, 3.4.

steps.annotation: Substitute and actually multiply -- don't eyeball. 7.20 is not 7.44, so cross off 3.
Break the multiplication into friendly pieces so the decimal work stays honest.
The left side lands EXACTLY on the right side -- not close, equal.
One exact match is the solution. With decimals, only the computation can tell 3.1 from 3.4.

faded_example.stem: Which value of n makes n + 1.35 = 4 true? Choices: 2.65, 2.75, 3.35.

steps.math: Try n = 3.35:  3.35 + 1.35 = 4.70, not 4 -- cross it off
steps.annotation: The first test is done for you: substitute, add exactly, compare.
Test n = 2.75. Line up the decimal points and add carefully. Does it land exactly on 4?
Test n = 2.65 and write the true equation you get.

skills.name: Select all equations from a list that have a given solution

prerequisite_skill.description: Substitute one fixed value into many different equations and verify each one.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Which of these equations are true when y = 4: y + 3 = 7, 2y = 9, y - 1 = 3?

skills.i_do_script: Think of the given value as one key and each equation as its own locked door -- the key might open one door, three doors, or none at all, and the only way to know is to try it in every single lock. On these items the value is fixed and you have a list of different equations — your student's job is to test that one value in every single equation and mark each one that turns out true. The trap is treating it like regular multiple choice and stopping at the first match. Coach them to slow down, work the list top to bottom, and only commit after every equation has been checked.

canonical_error.pattern: Student selects only one equation, treating the prompt like a single-answer multiple choice instead of select-all-that-apply, or only checks until they find the first match.
canonical_error.example: For 'select all equations with solution y = 4,' the student finds y + 3 = 7 is true, bubbles it, and stops without testing 2y = 8 or y - 1 = 3, missing two correct answers.
canonical_error.why: The student doesn't recognize multi-select format — they read 'select all' as 'pick one.' Or they understand the format but don't have a system for testing every option, so they quit early.

redirect_script.stop: Pause — how many can you pick?
redirect_script.prompt: Back to the key: you have only tried it in one lock -- how many doors are still sitting untested? Read the directions again — the word 'all' means you must test every choice. Number the equations 1 through 5 and check off each one as you substitute.
redirect_script.praise: Yes — you tested every option, not just the first one that worked.

vocabulary.definition: A value of the variable that makes the equation true.
A question where more than one answer can be correct — you mark every choice that fits.

worked_example_script.text: Hold up the value y = 4 like a single key, and lay the five equations A through E out on the desk like five locked doors in a hallway.
If the key opens door A, does that tell you anything at all about doors B, C, D, or E? Could one key open three of these doors? Could it open none?
Each door is its own separate test. The job is never 'find the first door that opens' -- it's 'try the key in all five locks and report every door that opened.'
Let's work this one together. The directions say: 'Select ALL equations that are true when y = 4.' Here is the list:  A) y + 3 = 7   B) 2y = 8   C) y - 1 = 3   D) y / 2 = 3   E) y + 5 = 10
Before we touch any numbers — what does the word 'all' tell us about how many answers we might pick? Could it be one, could it be more than one?
Good. So our value is y = 4 and it stays 4 the whole time. Let's start with A: y + 3 = 7. If I substitute 4 in for y, what do I write on the left side?
So we have 4 + 3 on the left and 7 on the right. Are those equal? Yes? Then is equation A true or false when y = 4?
Now B: 2y = 8. What does 2y mean when y is 4 — what number do we get on the left? And does it match the 8 on the right?
On to C: y - 1 = 3. Substitute 4 for y. What's the left side now, and is it equal to 3?
Here's where students often get tripped up. D says y / 2 = 3. If y is 4, what is 4 divided by 2? Does that match the 3 on the right?
And finally E: y + 5 = 10. Substitute 4. Does 4 + 5 equal 10?
We tested every single one. Which letters came out true — and how many are we bubbling in as our final answer?
Exactly — A, B, and C. The job wasn't to find one winner; it was to put 4 into every equation and keep every one that turned true. If we'd stopped at A, we'd have missed two correct answers.

practice_problems.stem: Is the equation y + 2 = 9 true when y = 7?
Is the equation 3y = 21 true when y = 6?
Select ALL the equations that are true when n = 5:  A) n + 4 = 9   B) 2n = 10   C) n - 3 = 1   D) 20 / n = 4   E) n + 5 = 55
practice_problems.notes: E baits students who paste digits together -- 5 next to 5 looks like 55.

practice_problems.stem: Select ALL the equations that are true when x = 8:  A) x - 5 = 3   B) x / 2 = 4   C) 3x = 32   D) x + 7 = 15
practice_problems.answer: A, B, and D. (C fails: 3 x 8 = 24, not 32.)

practice_problems.stem: Priya answered a select-all problem. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Select all equations with the solution y = 6.
practice_problems.answer: Priya stopped at the first true equation. Keep testing: B) 2 x 6 = 12 -- true. C) 6 - 6 = 0 -- true. All three are true, so the answer is A, B, and C.
practice_problems.notes: Bait for the canonical early-stopping error on multi-select items.

practice_problems.stem: Select ALL the equations that are true when m = 12:  A) m / 4 = 3   B) m + 8 = 22   C) m - 7 = 5   D) 2m = 24
practice_problems.answer: A, C, and D. (B fails: 12 + 8 = 20, not 22.)

practice_problems.stem: Write two different equations that are BOTH true when w = 9, using two different operations. Prove each one by substituting.
practice_problems.answer: Any correct pair, e.g. w + 1 = 10 (9 + 1 = 10) and 3w = 27 (3 x 9 = 27).
practice_problems.notes: Producing equations for a fixed value is the reverse of the test -- it shows the student owns the relationship.

practice_problems.stem: Exactly one of these is FALSE when k = 10:  A) k / 5 = 2   B) k + 15 = 25   C) 4k = 45   D) k - 9 = 1. Which one, and how do you know?
practice_problems.answer: C -- 4 x 10 = 40, not 45. The others all check out: 10 / 5 = 2, 10 + 15 = 25, 10 - 9 = 1.
practice_problems.notes: Hunting the one false statement forces a complete pass through the list.

activities.title: True or False when x = 4
materials: Equation cards (cut apart)
Two header cards: TRUE when x = 4 / FALSE when x = 4
activities.instructions:
1. The value is x = 4 for every single card -- write it at the top of the desk.
2. Partners alternate: draw a card, substitute 4 out loud, compute, and place it.
3. No card may be placed without the spoken check -- 'it looks true' doesn't count.
4. Debrief: how is this different from a question with one right answer?

activities.title: Why Did Priya Stop?
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show Priya's work and ask the group what she did RIGHT first (her check on A was perfect).
2. Ask: what did the directions ask for that Priya's answer doesn't deliver?
3. Have the group finish her job -- test B and C in writing.
4. Each student writes a rule for select-all problems that starts with 'Never stop until...'

content.worked_problem: Select all equations with solution y = 6: A) y + 4 = 10, B) 2y = 12, C) y - 6 = 0. Priya tested A, found it true, and answered 'A.'
content.error_step: Priya treated a select-ALL prompt like single-answer multiple choice and quit after her first success.
content.why: On multi-select items every choice is its own true/false question. B and C are also true when y = 6 (2 x 6 = 12 and 6 - 6 = 0), so stopping early left two correct answers on the table.

activities.title: Checklist Challenge
materials: One sheet per pair: five equations and one value
Pencils
activities.instructions:
1. Each pair gets the same five equations and one value (e.g., n = 7).
2. Speed matters, but a finish only counts if EVERY equation has a written substitution and a T or F next to it -- five checks, no blanks.
3. First complete-and-correct checklist wins the round; incomplete sheets are sent back.
4. Debrief: on the real test, what does the word 'all' force you to do before bubbling?

strategy_links.why: Partners must agree on every one of the five checks before committing -- Think-Pair-Share builds the test-everything habit socially.
Whiteboard Pass exposes who tested all five equations and who bubbled after one success.
Priya's early-stop is a clean, analyzable error that names the multi-select trap directly.

questioning_prompts: How many answers could a 'select all' question have -- one? three? zero?
Which equations have you tested so far? Show me your checkmarks.
You found one true equation. Are you done? How do you know?
What stays the same in every check on this problem, and what changes?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student selects only one equation, treating the prompt like single-answer multiple choice, or stops checking at the first match.
misconception_redirects.say: Read the directions again — the word 'all' means you must test every choice. Number the equations 1 through 5 and check off each one as you substitute.
misconception_redirects.praise: Yes — you tested every option, not just the first one that worked.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student marks an equation true because the test value appears somewhere in it -- picking y - 6 = 1 when y = 6 'because there's a 6 in it.'
misconception_redirects.say: Seeing the number isn't a test. Write 6 in place of y, compute the left side, and say the comparison out loud: 6 minus 6 is 0 -- is 0 equal to 1?
misconception_redirects.praise: That's it -- the substitution decided, not the way the equation looked.

quick_checks.prompt: n = 3. True or false, one at a time: n + 6 = 9? 2n = 5?
quick_checks.look_for: First true (3 + 6 = 9), second false (2 x 3 = 6, not 5) -- each judged on its own. Matching answers to each other signals the student isn't testing independently.

quick_checks.prompt: A select-all problem has five choices. How many must you check before you answer?
quick_checks.look_for: 'All five.' Any smaller number means early stopping is still the habit.

sentence_starters: I substituted ___ into every equation, and ___ of them came out true.
Equation ___ is false because the left side is ___, not ___.

worked_solution.stem: Select all the equations with the solution y = 4:  A) y + 3 = 7   B) 2y = 8   C) y - 1 = 3   D) y / 2 = 4

steps.annotation: Substitute 4 for y and compare. Mark it, but keep going -- 'all' means every choice gets tested.
Same value, new equation, same test. Both pass.
D fails even though it 'contains a 4.' The substitution decides, not the look of the equation.
Three winners -- if we had stopped at A, we'd have missed two of them.

faded_example.stem: Select all the equations with the solution x = 6:  A) x + 2 = 8   B) 3x = 20   C) x - 4 = 2

steps.math: A:  6 + 2 = 8 -- true. Mark A and keep testing.
steps.annotation: One success never ends a select-all problem.
Test B: what is 3 x 6? Does it equal 20?
Test C, then list every letter that turned out true.

skills.name: Decide Yes or No for each value of a variable in an inequality

prerequisite_skill.description: Read an inequality (using <, >, less-than-or-equal, greater-than-or-equal) and decide whether a given numeric statement is true.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Is the statement 4.7 > 5.1 true or false? How do you know?

skills.i_do_script: On this kind of item you get one inequality at the top and a little table of values, and your job is to mark Yes or No for each row on its own. We're going to walk through one row at a time together, and the symbol in the inequality is going to do most of the deciding for us.

canonical_error.pattern: Student treats < and > as if they always mean 'less than' or always mean the same thing, ignoring which side of the symbol the variable is on, or confuses strict < with less-than-or-equal at the boundary value.
canonical_error.example: For c < 6.4, the student marks c = 6.4 as 'Yes' because 'it's the same number,' missing that strict < excludes equality.
canonical_error.why: The student has not internalized the strict-vs-inclusive distinction. At the boundary value the symbol matters, and the student doesn't slow down to check.

redirect_script.stop: Wait — does the symbol allow equal?
redirect_script.prompt: Point at the symbol. If it's < or >, equal is NOT allowed. If it has a line under it, equal IS allowed. Re-decide that row with the symbol in mind.
redirect_script.praise: Right — you read the symbol carefully before answering.

vocabulary.definition: A statement that compares two expressions with <, >, less-than-or-equal, or greater-than-or-equal.
The comparison is correct after you substitute the value.
Uses < or > — equal values do NOT make the statement true.

worked_example_script.text: Let's look at this inequality together: c < 6.4. Underneath it is a table with three values to test: c = 5.0, c = 6.4, and c = 7.1. For each one we have to decide Yes (it makes the inequality true) or No (it doesn't).
Before we put any number in, read the inequality out loud with me. The symbol is the 'less than' sign — what is c < 6.4 asking us about any number we plug in for c?
Let's start with the first row, c = 5.0. If we put 5.0 in place of c, the statement becomes 5.0 < 6.4. Is 5.0 actually less than 6.4? So what do we write in that row, Yes or No?

Now the tricky row: c = 6.4. Substitute it in — the statement becomes 6.4 < 6.4. Look carefully at the symbol. It's a strict less-than, no line under it. Is 6.4 less than itself, or is it equal to itself? Does 'equal' count as a Yes here?

That boundary row is exactly where students get tripped up, so the move is: whenever the test value matches the number on the other side, look back at the symbol and ask 'does this symbol allow equal?' Strict < and > say no; the ones with a line underneath say yes.
Last row: c = 7.1. Substitute to get 7.1 < 6.4. Is 7.1 less than 6.4? So what goes in that row?
Read the table back to me — Yes, No, No. Notice each row stands on its own; one row's answer didn't change the next. What's the one question we asked ourselves on every single row?
Now you try one. Inequality: x greater-than-or-equal-to 8. Test x = 7, x = 8, and x = 12. Fill in Yes or No for each row, and pay extra attention to x = 8 — check the symbol before you decide.

practice_problems.stem: Is the statement 5 < 8 true?
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- 5 is less than 8.

practice_problems.stem: If x = 3, is the inequality x > 1 true?
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- substitute: 3 > 1 is a true statement.

practice_problems.stem: For the inequality n < 7.5, decide Yes or No for each value: n = 6.9, n = 7.5, n = 8.1.
practice_problems.answer: n = 6.9: Yes. n = 7.5: No -- 7.5 is not LESS than itself; strict < excludes equal. n = 8.1: No.
practice_problems.notes: The middle row is the boundary trap -- watch what students do at exactly 7.5.

practice_problems.stem: For the inequality c >= 4.2, decide Yes or No for each value: c = 4.2, c = 3.9.
practice_problems.answer: c = 4.2: Yes -- the symbol has a line under it, so equal counts. c = 3.9: No -- 3.9 is less than 4.2.

practice_problems.stem: Leo filled in one row of a Yes/No table. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Leo: 'Yes -- 9.3 is the same number, so of course it works.'
practice_problems.answer: No is correct. Substitute: 9.3 < 9.3 asks 'is 9.3 LESS than 9.3?' It isn't -- it's equal, and strict < does not allow equal. Equal only counts with <= or >=.
practice_problems.notes: Direct bait for the canonical strict-vs-inclusive boundary error.

practice_problems.stem: For the inequality x > 2.75, decide Yes or No for each value: x = 2.8, x = 2.7, x = 2.75.
practice_problems.answer: x = 2.8: Yes (2.8 = 2.80, which is more than 2.75). x = 2.7: No (2.70 < 2.75). x = 2.75: No -- strict > excludes equal.
practice_problems.notes: 2.8 vs 2.75 also catches students who think 'more digits means bigger.'

practice_problems.stem: Give a value that makes x <= 5 true but makes x < 5 false. Explain why the same number gets two different answers.
practice_problems.answer: Exactly 5. The statement 5 <= 5 is true because <= allows equal; 5 < 5 is false because strict < does not. The symbol, not the number, made the difference.
practice_problems.notes: Explain-the-contrast shows the symbol distinction is owned, not memorized.

practice_problems.stem: Mark 4.1 on the number line. Does y = 4.1 make the inequality y > 3.5 true? How does the picture show it?
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- 4.1 sits to the right of 3.5 on the line, and 'to the right' is what > means.
practice_problems.notes: The number line turns the symbol into a position -- useful for every later inequality skill.

activities.title: Boundary Line-Up
materials: Painter's tape line on the desk or floor
Index cards with values written large
One card marking the boundary number
activities.instructions:
1. Tape a line and place the boundary card (say, 6.4) at the center. Announce the inequality: c < 6.4.
2. Deal value cards (5.0, 6.39, 6.4, 6.41, 7.1...). Each student places their card on the YES side, the NO side, or ON the boundary.
3. The boundary card holder must argue their case; the group votes, then checks the symbol together.
4. Switch the inequality to c <= 6.4 and ask: whose card just changed sides? Why only that one?
5. Debrief: what's the only value on the whole line that cares whether the symbol has a line under it?

activities.title: Symbol Says
materials: Statement cards and Yes/No cards (cut apart)
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the statement cards face up. Each shows an inequality and one test value.
2. Partners take turns matching each statement to Yes or No -- saying the substituted statement out loud first ('is 5 less than or equal to 5?').
3. Every match must name the symbol: strict or has-a-line-under-it.
4. Debrief: which matches were decided by the symbol alone?

activities.title: Leo at the Boundary
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show Leo's row and let the group debate before you say anything.
2. Ask: what is Leo's reasoning? (It's almost right -- the numbers DO match.)
3. Have the group read t < 9.3 out loud as a question: 'is 9.3 LESS than 9.3?'
4. Then flip the symbol to <= and re-vote. Each student writes the one-sentence rule for boundary values.

content.worked_problem: Inequality t < 9.3, row t = 9.3. Leo marked Yes 'because 9.3 is the same number.'
content.error_step: Leo treated 'equal to the boundary' as automatically true, ignoring that strict < excludes equality.
content.why: Substituting gives 9.3 < 9.3, which asks whether 9.3 is LESS than itself -- it isn't. Equal values only satisfy the symbols with a line underneath (<= and >=).

strategy_links.why: A number line makes the boundary concrete: Yes-values live on one side, and the boundary point itself belongs only to <= and >=.
Fast choral rounds of 'does the symbol allow equal -- yes or no?' automate the strict-vs-inclusive read this skill hinges on.
Leo's boundary error is the exact misconception -- analyzing it turns the symbol check into an explicit habit.

questioning_prompts: Read the symbol out loud -- does it allow the two sides to be equal?
Where does this value sit compared to the boundary number -- left or right on the number line?
Does your answer for this row change anything about the next row? Why not?
Which value in this table forces you to look hardest at the symbol?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student marks the boundary value Yes under a strict < or >, saying 'it's the same number,' or mixes up which symbols allow equality.
misconception_redirects.say: Point at the symbol. If it's < or >, equal is NOT allowed. If it has a line under it, equal IS allowed. Re-decide that row with the symbol in mind.
misconception_redirects.praise: Right — you read the symbol carefully before answering.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reads the inequality backwards -- treating c < 6.4 as 'c is bigger than 6.4.'
misconception_redirects.say: Read it left to right while pointing: 'c... is less than... 6.4.' The small pointed end of the symbol always faces the smaller side. Now re-test your value.
misconception_redirects.praise: Good -- you read the statement in order and let the symbol point the way.

quick_checks.prompt: x >= 6: does x = 6 make it true, yes or no?
quick_checks.look_for: An instant yes -- the line under the symbol allows equal. A no means strict-vs-inclusive is still fuzzy; run the boundary line-up again.

quick_checks.prompt: x < 10: yes or no for x = 10.5?
quick_checks.look_for: No, with '10.5 is more than 10.' A yes signals either a backwards read of the symbol or a decimal comparison slip.

sentence_starters: The symbol ___ does / does not allow equal, so the boundary value gets a ___.
___ makes the inequality ___ because it is ___ than ___.

worked_solution.stem: Inequality: c < 6.4. Decide Yes or No for each value: c = 5.0, c = 6.4, c = 7.1.

steps.annotation: Substitute and read the new statement as a question. 5.0 sits below 6.4, so this row is a Yes.
The boundary row. Strict < asks for LESS than -- equal doesn't count. Only <= or >= would let 6.4 in.
7.1 is above the boundary, so it fails. Each row was its own separate test.

faded_example.stem: Inequality: x >= 8. Decide Yes or No for each value: x = 7, x = 8, x = 12.
faded_example.answer: x = 7: No.  x = 8: Yes.  x = 12: Yes.

steps.math: x = 7:  is 7 >= 8?  No -- 7 is less than 8.
steps.annotation: The first row is done for you: substitute, read the question, answer it.
x = 8 is the boundary. Look at the symbol first -- does >= allow equal?
Test x = 12: substitute, compare, and write Yes or No.

skills.name: Select all inequalities from a list for which a given number is a solution

prerequisite_skill.description: Substitute one fixed number into multiple inequalities and judge each one.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Which of these are true when x = 11: x < 1, x > 10, x > 14?

skills.i_do_script: On this kind of problem the number stays the same and the inequalities change — your job is to plug that one number into every inequality and see which ones turn out to be true statements. The trap is picking an inequality just because the numbers in it 'look close' to your test number, so we're going to slow down and let substitution do the deciding. I'll ask the questions; you do the testing out loud, one inequality at a time.

canonical_error.pattern: Student picks an inequality based on which numbers 'look close' to the test value, instead of substituting and comparing — especially confusing > with < when the variable side is read out of order.
canonical_error.example: For 'select inequalities where 11 is a solution,' the student picks x > 14 because 14 is closest in size to 11, missing that 11 > 14 is false.
canonical_error.why: The student reads the inequality as a numeric proximity question rather than as a comparison. They see '14' near '11' and assume similarity equals truth, instead of substituting 11 in and checking the direction of the symbol.

redirect_script.prompt: Write the test number in place of the variable in each inequality, then read the new statement out loud and ask, 'Is this true?' Cross out the ones that turn false.
redirect_script.praise: Excellent — you let substitution decide, not appearance.

vocabulary.definition: A value that makes the inequality true when substituted.
A comparison statement using <, >, less-than-or-equal, or greater-than-or-equal.

worked_example_script.text: Here's the problem: 'Select all inequalities for which x = 11 is a solution.' The choices are x < 1, x > 10, x > -7, x < -2, and x > 14.
The number 11 is fixed and the inequalities change. What do you think we have to do to each inequality to figure out if 11 is a solution?
Let's start with the first one, x < 1. If we put 11 in place of x, what statement do we get? Read it out loud — is 11 less than 1?
Next: x > 10. Substitute 11 for x. What statement do we get, and is it true or false?
Now x > -7. Plug in 11. Is 11 greater than negative 7? Picture the number line — which one is further to the right?
Try x < -2. Replace x with 11. Is 11 less than negative 2? True or false?
Last one: x > 14. The numbers 11 and 14 look close, but don't trust appearance — substitute. Is 11 actually greater than 14?
Look back at all five. Which ones turned into true statements when we put 11 in? Those are the ones we select — and what did we do every single time before deciding?

practice_problems.stem: Is the statement 9 > 4 true?
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- 9 is greater than 4.

practice_problems.stem: If x = 12, is the inequality x < 20 true?
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- substitute: 12 < 20 is true.

practice_problems.stem: Select ALL the inequalities for which 15 is a solution:  A) x > 9   B) x < 15   C) x > 20   D) x < 32
practice_problems.answer: A and D. (B fails: 15 < 15 is false -- strict. C fails: 15 > 20 is false.)
practice_problems.notes: B is the boundary trap inside a select-all -- two skills colliding on purpose.

practice_problems.stem: Select the two inequalities for which 7 is a solution:  A) x < 3   B) x > 5   C) x > 12   D) x < 10
practice_problems.answer: B and D. (7 > 5 is true and 7 < 10 is true; 7 < 3 and 7 > 12 are both false.)

practice_problems.stem: Ava picked her answers by how close the numbers looked. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Select the inequalities for which 11 is a solution.
Ava: '11 is bigger than 10, so A works. And 14 is really close to 11, so B probably works too.'
practice_problems.answer: Only A. Substitute into each: 11 > 10 is true, but 11 > 14 asks whether 11 is greater than 14 -- it isn't. Close is not a solution; only the substituted statement being TRUE counts.
practice_problems.notes: Bait for the canonical proximity error -- 'the numbers look close' replaces the actual test.

practice_problems.stem: Select ALL the inequalities for which 6 is a solution:  A) x >= 6   B) x > 6   C) x <= 8   D) x < 5
practice_problems.answer: A and C. (A: 6 >= 6 is true -- equal is allowed. B: 6 > 6 is false -- strict. C: 6 <= 8 is true. D: 6 < 5 is false.)

practice_problems.stem: Write one inequality that has 20 as a solution and one that does not. Prove both with substitution.
practice_problems.answer: Any correct pair, e.g. x > 12 (20 > 12 -- true) and x < 8 (20 < 8 -- false).
practice_problems.notes: Producing inequalities reverses the direction -- the student authors the test instead of just running it.

practice_problems.stem: Mark 11 on the number line. Which statement is true: 11 > 14 or 11 > 10? How does the picture show it?
practice_problems.answer: 11 > 10 is true -- on the line, 11 sits to the right of 10 but to the LEFT of 14, so 11 > 14 is false.
practice_problems.notes: The picture defeats the 'close means true' instinct: position, not distance, decides.

activities.title: Is 12 In or Out?
materials: Inequality cards (cut apart)
Two header cards: 12 IS a solution / 12 is NOT a solution
activities.instructions:
1. The test number is 12 for every card -- write '12' big at the top of the desk.
2. Partners alternate: draw an inequality, substitute 12 out loud ('is 12 greater than 25?'), and place the card.
3. A placement only counts with the spoken statement -- 'the numbers are close' is not a reason.
4. Debrief: which card LOOKED like a solution but wasn't, and what saved you?

activities.title: Ava's Close Call
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show Ava's work. Ask what she did right first (A was tested honestly).
2. Ask: what does 'close' mean in Ava's sentence about B -- and is 'close' something an inequality can be?
3. Have the group substitute 11 into x > 14 and read the statement out loud.
4. Each student writes Ava a one-line rule that starts with 'An inequality is only true if...'

content.worked_problem: Select the inequalities for which 11 is a solution: A) x > 10, B) x > 14. Ava picked A and B because '14 is really close to 11.'
content.error_step: Ava judged B by how near 14 is to 11 instead of substituting and reading the direction of the symbol.
content.why: Substitution gives 11 > 14 -- 'is 11 greater than 14?' -- which is false no matter how close the numbers are. Truth comes from the comparison's direction, not the distance between the numbers.

activities.title: Solution Scramble
materials: Inequality cards posted around the room
One target number on the board
activities.instructions:
1. Post 8-10 inequality cards around the room and write one target number (say, 16) on the board.
2. Teams walk the room and collect ONLY the inequalities the target number satisfies.
3. Back at base, each capture must be defended with a spoken substitution: '16 < 40 -- true, keep it.'
4. A wrong capture costs two points; a missed solution costs one -- so testing beats grabbing.
5. Debrief: why is 'the numbers look close' the most expensive mistake in this game?

strategy_links.why: Each partner must voice the substituted statement ('is 11 greater than 14?') before the pair commits -- talk exposes proximity-guessing instantly.
Rapid choral true/false rounds on substituted statements build the reflex of reading the symbol's direction instead of eyeballing distances.
Whiteboard Pass shows every student's substitution on every choice, so a 'close enough' pick can't hide in the crowd.

questioning_prompts: What number are you plugging in, and where exactly does it go?
Read the statement AFTER substituting. Is it true?
Did you pick that one because the statement is true, or because the numbers look close?
Which direction does the symbol point -- which side has to be bigger?
How many are you supposed to select? Where do the directions say so?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student picks an inequality because its numbers 'look close' to the test value -- like choosing x > 14 for the number 11 -- instead of substituting and comparing.
misconception_redirects.say: Write the test number in place of the variable in each inequality, then read the new statement out loud and ask, 'Is this true?' Cross out the ones that turn false.
misconception_redirects.praise: Excellent — you let substitution decide, not appearance.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student selects only one inequality when the stem says 'select the two' or 'select all.'
misconception_redirects.say: Circle the words in the directions that tell you how many. Then test every choice with a written substitution before you commit to any of them.
misconception_redirects.praise: That's the discipline -- every choice tested, count double-checked.

quick_checks.look_for: No -- strict > excludes equal. A yes means the boundary rule from the table skill didn't transfer to this format.
Yes -- 11 sits far to the right of -7 on the number line; no computation with negatives needed. A no signals trouble comparing against a negative number.

sentence_starters: When I put ___ in for x, the statement says ___, which is ___.
I rejected ___ because ___ is not ___ than ___.

worked_solution.stem: Select the two inequalities in which 11 is a solution:  A) x < 1   B) x > 10   C) x < 32   D) x > 14

steps.annotation: Substitute 11 for x and read the statement as a question. 11 is nowhere near below 1 -- cross it off.

steps.math: B:  is 11 > 10?  True.   C:  is 11 < 32?  True
steps.annotation: Both substituted statements are true -- keep them. Notice we keep testing after the first success.
14 looks 'close' to 11, but close isn't the question -- 11 sits LEFT of 14, so it is not greater.
Exactly two true statements, found by substituting into all four -- never by eyeballing.

faded_example.stem: Select the two inequalities in which 9 is a solution:  A) x > 3   B) x < 9   C) x < 15

steps.annotation: The first test is modeled: substitute, read, decide.
Test B: the statement becomes 9 < 9. Check the symbol before you answer.
Test C, then name the two inequalities you're keeping.

skills.name: Identify which set of numbers contains only solutions to an inequality

prerequisite_skill.description: Substitute several values into one inequality and judge whether all of them satisfy it.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: For x < 1/2, are all of {1/6, 2/5, 1/3, 1/2} solutions? Which one is not?

skills.i_do_script: On these problems the inequality stays put and four different sets of numbers are offered as candidates. Our job is to find the set where every single number inside makes the inequality true — even one bad number disqualifies the whole set. Don't let students settle for 'most of them work'; push them to test every member.

canonical_error.pattern: Student picks the set that has the most solutions instead of the set where every member is a solution — they treat 'mostly true' as 'true.'
canonical_error.example: For x < 1/2, the student picks {1/6, 2/5, 1/3, 1/2} because three of four work, missing that 1/2 fails and only the set where all four members are below 1/2 is correct.
canonical_error.why: The student is using a 'majority rules' heuristic rather than a universal rule. They have not internalized that 'contains only solutions' is a quantifier — every element must satisfy, not just most.

redirect_script.stop: Stop — even one wrong number disqualifies the set.
redirect_script.prompt: For each set, draw four boxes and check off each number against the inequality. The first time you get a 'no,' cross out the entire set and move to the next one.
redirect_script.praise: Yes — you required every number to work, not just most of them.

vocabulary.definition: A group of numbers listed inside braces, like {1/6, 2/5, 1/3}.
A value that makes the inequality true.
In 'contains only solutions,' the word 'only' means every single number must be a solution — no exceptions.

worked_example_script.text: Here is the inequality: x < 1/2. And here is one of the candidate sets: {1/6, 2/5, 1/3, 1/2}.
Before we test anything, what does the question want from this whole set? In your own words, what has to be true about the numbers inside the braces?
Let's start with the first number, 1/6. If we substitute it for x, what statement do we get, and is it true?
Now try 2/5 in place of x. Is 2/5 less than 1/2? How can you tell — what's a quick way to compare those two fractions?
Keep going with 1/3. Is 1/3 < 1/2 a true statement?
Last one in the set: 1/2. When we substitute, we get 1/2 < 1/2. Is that true or false? Watch the symbol carefully — does < allow the two sides to be equal?
So three of the four numbers worked, but one didn't. Based on what the question asked for, can we keep this set as our answer? Why or why not?

Right — the word 'only' means every number has to be a solution. As soon as one number fails, the whole set is out, no matter how many others worked. On a real item you'd now move to the next candidate set and repeat the same check until you find the one where all four numbers pass.

practice_problems.stem: Is the statement 1/4 < 1/2 true?
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- one fourth is smaller than one half. (In fourths: 1/4 < 2/4.)

practice_problems.stem: If x = 2/3, is the inequality x > 1/2 true? Compare using sixths.
Does the set {2, 5, 7} contain only solutions to x < 8?
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- test all three: 2 < 8, 5 < 8, and 7 < 8 are all true, so every member passes.

practice_problems.stem: Does the set {3, 6, 9} contain only solutions to x > 4?
practice_problems.answer: No -- 3 > 4 is false. One failure disqualifies the whole set, even though 6 and 9 both work.

practice_problems.stem: Sam checked a set against an inequality. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Sam: '1/6 works, 2/5 works, 1/3 works. Three out of four -- good enough. This is the set.'
practice_problems.answer: 'Contains ONLY solutions' means every single number must pass. The fourth number fails: 1/2 < 1/2 is false because strict < excludes equal. This set is disqualified -- 'good enough' isn't a category.
practice_problems.notes: Bait for the canonical majority-rules error, with the boundary fraction as the failing member.

practice_problems.stem: Which set contains only solutions to x > 1/3?  A) {1/2, 2/3, 1/4}   B) {2/5, 1/2, 5/6}
practice_problems.notes: The failing member is buried last in a set of mostly-solutions -- exactly the trap format.

practice_problems.stem: Mark 1/6, 2/5, and 1/2 on the number line (use the tick labels to place them). Which of the three make x < 1/2 true?
practice_problems.answer: 1/6 and 2/5 -- both sit to the left of 1/2 on the line (2/5 = 0.4). The point at 1/2 itself does not count: strict < excludes the boundary.
practice_problems.notes: Placing the fractions makes the 'left of the boundary' picture do the comparing.

practice_problems.stem: Build your own set of three fractions that contains only solutions to x < 3/4, then prove each member with a comparison.
practice_problems.notes: Producing a qualifying set forces the all-members test in reverse.

activities.title: Good Enough Isn't
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show Sam's 'three out of four' reasoning and let the group react first.
2. Ask: in everyday life, is 3 out of 4 usually good enough? Why does math's word 'only' change the rules?
3. Have the group test the fourth number, 1/2, out loud against x < 1/2.
4. Each student writes the rule: 'A set contains only solutions when ___.'

content.worked_problem: Which set contains only solutions to x < 1/2? Sam picked {1/6, 2/5, 1/3, 1/2} because three of the four numbers work.
content.error_step: Sam treated 'mostly solutions' as 'only solutions' and never let the one failure disqualify the set.
content.why: 'Only' is all-or-nothing: every member must make the inequality true. 1/2 < 1/2 is false (strict < excludes equal), so the set is out no matter how many members passed.

activities.title: One Bad Apple
materials: Sets of 4 number cards in envelopes (one envelope per group)
One red chip per group
The inequality written on the board
activities.instructions:
1. Write one inequality on the board (e.g., x < 3/4). Give each group an envelope holding a 4-number set.
2. The group tests members one at a time, saying each comparison out loud.
3. The moment ANY member fails, the red chip goes on the envelope -- that set is done; no need to test the rest. If all four pass, the envelope is a keeper.
4. Groups swap envelopes and re-verify each other's verdicts.
5. Debrief: how many failures does it take to kill a set, and how many passes does it take to keep one?

activities.title: Set Detective
materials: Board with one inequality and four candidate sets
Mini whiteboards
activities.instructions:
1. Post an inequality and four sets, exactly one of which contains only solutions.
2. Pairs race to find the failing member in each wrong set -- the fastest LEGAL kill wins, where legal means the comparison is written out.
3. The winning set must be verified member by member before a pair can claim it.
4. Debrief: why is finding one failure so much faster than proving all four members pass?

strategy_links.why: The majority-rules error is subtle and feels reasonable -- analyzing Sam's 'three out of four' work is the fastest way to make 'only' mean only.
Partners debating keep-or-toss on each set must voice every member's test, which blocks silent 'mostly works' shortcuts.
Thinking aloud through one full set -- including stopping the instant a member fails -- models the all-or-nothing check as an efficient routine.

questioning_prompts: What does the word 'only' demand of every number in the set?
How many members must you test before you can KEEP a set? How many failures before you can TOSS one?
Which number in this set is doing the most work -- the one closest to the boundary?
How are you comparing these two fractions -- common denominator, benchmark, or a picture?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student picks the set with the MOST solutions instead of the set where every member is a solution -- treating 'mostly true' as 'true.'
misconception_redirects.say: For each set, draw four boxes and check off each number against the inequality. The first time you get a 'no,' cross out the entire set and move to the next one.
misconception_redirects.praise: Yes — you required every number to work, not just most of them.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student compares fractions by denominator size alone -- deciding 1/6 > 1/2 'because 6 is bigger than 2.'
misconception_redirects.say: A bigger denominator means MORE pieces, so each piece is smaller. Rewrite both fractions with a common denominator, or place both on one number line, then compare.
misconception_redirects.praise: Good -- you compared the actual sizes, not the digits.

quick_checks.prompt: The set {1, 3, 5} against x < 5 -- keep it or toss it?
quick_checks.look_for: Toss -- 5 < 5 is false, and one failure disqualifies. Keeping it reveals either the boundary error or majority-rules thinking; ask which member they tested last.

quick_checks.prompt: How many failures does it take to disqualify a set?
quick_checks.look_for: 'One.' Any other answer means the quantifier hasn't landed -- rerun One Bad Apple.

sentence_starters: I tossed set ___ because ___ fails the inequality.
Every number in set ___ passes: ___, ___, and ___ are all ___ than ___.

worked_solution.stem: Which set contains only solutions to the inequality x < 1/2?  A) {1/6, 2/5, 1/3, 1/2}   B) {1/6, 2/5, 1/3, 1/4}

steps.math: A:  1/6, 2/5, and 1/3 all pass... but 1/2 < 1/2 is false
steps.annotation: Test every member. Three passes don't matter -- one failure disqualifies the whole set. 'Only' is all-or-nothing.
Compare fractions honestly -- rewrite with a common denominator when the sizes aren't obvious.
Keep testing until EVERY member has passed. A set is only safe after the last check.

steps.math: All four members of B pass -> B
steps.annotation: That's what 'contains only solutions' means: no exceptions.

faded_example.stem: Which set contains only solutions to x > 2?  A) {3, 5, 2}   B) {4, 6, 9}

steps.math: A:  3 > 2 true, 5 > 2 true, but 2 > 2 is false -- toss set A
steps.annotation: One failure ends the set, even at the very last member.
Test every number in set B against x > 2. Any failures?
State the winning set and finish the sentence: 'Every member passes because...'

skills.name: Use substitution to test combinations in a real-world inequality and justify the choice

prerequisite_skill.description: Substitute two values for two different variables in a given inequality and decide whether the resulting statement is true.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Given 340 + 30a + 45g less-than-or-equal-to 2000, is a = 16, g = 23 a safe load? Show the substitution.

skills.i_do_script: This problem hands us a story and an inequality already written for us — we don't have to build it, we just have to test combinations. Instead of me telling you what to plug in, I'll ask questions and let you decide what counts as a valid load. Pay attention to what the inequality is really asking and where each number from the story belongs.

canonical_error.pattern: Student tries to 'solve' the real-world inequality algebraically or write a new inequality from scratch, instead of just substituting each given combination and checking.
canonical_error.example: Given 340 + 30a + 45g less-than-or-equal-to 2000, the student tries to isolate a or g, gets stuck, and guesses Part A without ever plugging the candidate combinations in.
canonical_error.why: The student doesn't recognize that this is still a substitution-and-verify task. The story makes them think they need to 'set up' or 'solve,' but the inequality is already provided — the only real work is substitution and checking.

redirect_script.stop: Hang on — the inequality is already there.
redirect_script.prompt: Underline the inequality on the page. For each answer choice, write a substitution: replace a and g with the numbers in that choice, compute the left side, and compare to the right side. Pick the choices that fit.
redirect_script.praise: Nice — you trusted substitution to do the work.

vocabulary.definition: Replacing every variable in an expression or inequality with a specific number.
A combination of values that makes the inequality true when substituted.
Show your substitution and the resulting comparison so the reader can see why your answer is true.

next_steps.if_pass: Student has mastered 6.AF.2 across all four proficiency bands.

worked_example_script.text: Display the scenario: 'A delivery truck weighs 340 pounds when empty. It carries crates of apples (30 pounds each) and crates of oranges (45 pounds each). The total weight cannot exceed 2000 pounds. The inequality is 340 + 30a + 45g less-than-or-equal-to 2000. Part A: Which combination is a safe load — (a=16, g=23) or (a=20, g=30)? Part B: Justify your answer.'
Before we touch any numbers, look at the inequality. What does the letter a stand for in this story, and what does the letter g stand for?

Good. Now look at the symbol in the middle — it's less-than-or-equal-to 2000. In plain English, what is that symbol telling the truck it's allowed to do? Can the load weigh exactly 2000? Can it weigh 2001?
Let's test the first combination: 16 crates of apples, 23 crates of oranges. Where does the 16 go in the inequality, and where does the 23 go? Don't compute yet — just point.
Now compute the left side. What is 340 + 30 times 16 + 45 times 23?
You got 1855. Compare it to 2000 using the symbol from the inequality. Is 1855 less than or equal to 2000 — yes or no? So is this combination a safe load?
Now do the same thing for the second combination: a = 20, g = 30. Substitute, compute the left side, and compare to 2000. What do you get, and is it safe?
For Part B, the question wants you to justify. What sentences would you write to show a teacher exactly how you decided which combination was safe? Walk me through what you'd put on the page.

If the student tries to solve for a or g, or starts writing a new inequality, stop them. Point at the inequality on the page and say, 'It's already written. Your only job is to put the numbers in and check.' If they pick the unsafe combination because the numbers 'look bigger and that's more,' have them actually compute the left side out loud — the comparison only works after substitution, not by eyeballing the crate counts.

practice_problems.stem: In the inequality 340 + 30a + 45g <= 2000, what does the term 30a mean if a = 2?
practice_problems.answer: 30 x 2 = 60 -- two crates of apples at 30 pounds each contribute 60 pounds.

practice_problems.stem: If a = 10 and g = 0, what is the value of 340 + 30a + 45g?
A van's load must satisfy 200 + 20x + 30y <= 800. Is x = 10, y = 10 an allowed load?
A trailer's load must satisfy 150 + 25b + 40c <= 1000. Test the combination b = 12, c = 14.
practice_problems.answer: No -- 150 + 25(12) + 40(14) = 150 + 300 + 560 = 1010, and 1010 <= 1000 is false. Ten pounds over is still over.

practice_problems.stem: Jade got tangled up on this problem. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Jade: '40a = 1500 - 500, so a = 25. My a is only 15, so this combination doesn't work??'
practice_problems.answer: Jade tried to SOLVE the inequality -- and dropped g entirely. The job is substitution: 500 + 40(15) + 25(10) = 500 + 600 + 250 = 1350, and 1350 <= 1500 is true. The combination IS allowed.
practice_problems.notes: Bait for the canonical 'tries to solve instead of substitute' error.

practice_problems.stem: A freight elevator's load must satisfy 100 + 15p + 20q <= 400. Which combination is allowed: p = 8, q = 9 or p = 10, q = 8?
practice_problems.answer: p = 8, q = 9 -- the total is 100 + 120 + 180 = 400 exactly, and <= allows equal. The other combination totals 100 + 150 + 160 = 410, which is over.
practice_problems.notes: The allowed combination lands exactly ON the limit -- the strict-vs-inclusive idea returns in context.

practice_problems.stem: For the truck inequality 340 + 30a + 45g <= 2000, compute the total for a = 16, g = 23 and mark it on the number line. Is it on the safe side of 2000?
practice_problems.answer: 340 + 480 + 1035 = 1855. Mark 1855 -- it sits left of 2000, so the load is safe.
practice_problems.notes: Seeing the total sit left of the limit turns the abstract comparison into a picture.

practice_problems.stem: For 340 + 30a + 45g <= 2000, find your own combination of a and g whose total is within 50 pounds of the limit but still safe. Prove it.
practice_problems.notes: Designing a near-limit load requires running the substitution forward and backward.

practice_problems.stem: Write two sentences justifying why a = 16, g = 23 is a safe load for 340 + 30a + 45g <= 2000. Your justification must show the substitution.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: 'I substituted a = 16 and g = 23: 340 + 30(16) + 45(23) = 340 + 480 + 1035 = 1855. Since 1855 <= 2000 is true, the truck can carry this load safely.'
practice_problems.notes: This is the Part B skill -- the written justification IS the demonstration the standard asks for.

activities.title: Load the Truck
materials: Crate cards: apple crates marked 30 lb, orange crates marked 45 lb
One 'machine' card marked 340 lb
The inequality 340 + 30a + 45g <= 2000 on the board
Calculator-free scratch paper
activities.instructions:
1. Each group 'loads a truck' by choosing how many apple cards (a) and orange cards (g) to take -- the machine card is always on board.
2. The group computes the total with a written substitution: 340 + 30a + 45g.
3. Compare the total to 2000 and declare SAFE or OVERLOADED, recording each trial in a table.
4. Challenge round: build the heaviest load that is still safe.
5. Debrief: what did every safe check have in common? (A substitution, a total, and a comparison -- never algebra.)

activities.title: Don't Solve It -- Test It
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show Jade's work and ask: what was she trying to do? (Solve for a -- a skill from a different kind of problem.)
2. Ask: what information did Jade's approach throw away? (The g term, and the actual combination she was given.)
3. Have the group run the real test: substitute both values, compute the total, compare to 1500.
4. Each student writes the rule: 'When the inequality is already written and the values are given, my job is to ___.'

content.worked_problem: Inequality 500 + 40a + 25g <= 1500, testing a = 15, g = 10. Jade computed 40a = 1500 - 500 and concluded a = 25, so the combination 'doesn't work.'
content.error_step: Jade tried to solve the inequality algebraically instead of substituting the given combination -- and her rearrangement ignored the 25g term entirely.
content.why: This is still a substitution task: replace a with 15 and g with 10, compute 500 + 600 + 250 = 1350, and compare. 1350 <= 1500 is true, so the combination is allowed. Solving was never required -- and done Jade's way, it wasn't even valid.

activities.title: Limit Bouncer
materials: Mini whiteboards
One posted inequality with a story (e.g., 100 + 15p + 20q <= 400)
activities.instructions:
1. You're the club owner; students are bouncers at the door. Call out a combination: 'p = 8, q = 9 wants in!'
2. Every bouncer substitutes, computes the total, and writes ADMIT or BOUNCE with the total shown.
3. Boards up. One student defends the call by reading the full comparison out loud.
4. Sneak in a total that equals the limit exactly to test whether <= admits it.
5. Debrief: what's the only evidence a bouncer is allowed to use? (The computed total versus the limit.)

strategy_links.why: The two-variable check is a longer chain -- model it, run it together, then hand students the full substitute-compute-compare-justify sequence.
Thinking aloud while substituting two values keeps each letter attached to its number and makes the order of operations visible.
Contrasting a correct substitution with Jade's solve-it attempt shows why the given inequality plus given values means test, not solve.

questioning_prompts: What does each letter stand for in this story? Say it before you write anything.
Where does each number from the combination go in the inequality?
What total did you compute, and what does the symbol allow it to be?
Can the total equal the limit exactly and still be allowed? How do you know?
What would your written justification need to show a reader who hasn't done the problem?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student tries to 'solve' the real-world inequality algebraically or set up a new one, instead of substituting each given combination and checking.
misconception_redirects.say: Underline the inequality on the page. For each answer choice, write a substitution: replace a and g with the numbers in that choice, compute the left side, and compare to the right side. Pick the choices that fit.
misconception_redirects.praise: Nice — you trusted substitution to do the work.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student swaps the values -- putting the apple count where g is and the orange count where a is.
misconception_redirects.say: Touch each letter and say what it stands for out loud before you write. The a-number goes where a is; the g-number goes where g is. Rewrite the substitution with labels over each term.
misconception_redirects.praise: Good -- every number landed on its own variable.

quick_checks.look_for: 1090, yes -- a clean two-variable substitution. A wrong total signals an order-of-operations slip (adding before multiplying) or a swap.

quick_checks.prompt: Your total comes out exactly equal to the limit. Allowed or not?
quick_checks.look_for: Allowed -- <= includes equal. 'Not allowed' means the strict-vs-inclusive distinction didn't survive the trip into context.

sentence_starters: I substituted a = ___ and g = ___, and the total came out to ___.
The combination is / is not allowed because ___ <= ___ is ___.

worked_solution.stem: A truck can carry at most 2000 pounds: 340 + 30a + 45g <= 2000, where a is crates of apples and g is crates of oranges. Is a = 16, g = 23 a safe load?
worked_solution.answer: Yes -- the total is 1855, and 1855 <= 2000 is true.

steps.annotation: Replace each letter with its own number -- a gets 16, g gets 23. Nothing to solve; the inequality is already built.
Multiply first: 30 x 16 = 480 and 45 x 23 = 1035. Order of operations still runs the show.
Add the three pieces to get the load's total weight.

steps.math: 1855 <= 2000 -- true, so the load is safe
steps.annotation: Compare the total to the limit. The symbol allows anything up to AND including 2000 -- and 1855 is under. That comparison IS the justification.

faded_example.stem: Same truck: 340 + 30a + 45g <= 2000. Is a = 20, g = 30 a safe load?

steps.annotation: The substitution is done for you -- a is 20 and g is 30, each on its own variable.
Multiply both products, then add all three numbers. What total do you get?
Compare your total to 2000 using the symbol. Safe or not -- and write the one sentence that justifies your verdict.

looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching. Per the 6.AF.2 item spec, this concept is not specifically addressed in the Indiana Academic Standards prior to grade 6, so this column is intentionally empty.

on_grade.label: On Grade
on_grade.description: The standard's actual grade-level expectations — one sub-skill per engine stem covering Below, Approaching, At, and Above proficiency bands.

looking_forward.label: Looking Forward
looking_forward.description: Bridge to the next standard. Per the 6.AF.2 item spec, this concept is not specifically addressed in the Indiana Academic Standards in subsequent grade levels, so this column is intentionally empty.

progression.narrative: 6.AF.2 asks students to do one thing extremely well: treat substitution as a TEST. An equation or inequality with a variable in it isn't a command to solve -- it's a true/false question waiting for a number, and the student's job is to put each candidate value in, compute exactly, and let the comparison decide. The arc starts where the test feels safest: one whole-number equation and a short list of candidates (S0), so the substitute-compute-compare loop becomes automatic before anything else changes. Then the numbers get less friendly -- decimals where 'looks close' fails and only exact computation settles it (S1) -- and the frame flips: one fixed value tested against many equations, which introduces select-all discipline (S2). From there the standard moves to its real center of gravity, inequalities: judging each value in a table on its own, with the strict-versus-inclusive symbol doing the deciding at the boundary (S3), then one number tested against many inequalities where the direction of the symbol, not number proximity, determines truth (S4). The 'specified set' language of the standard lands in S5 -- a set counts only if EVERY member passes, an all-or-nothing quantifier students must own. Finally S6 stretches the same loop to a real-world inequality with two variables, where students substitute a combination, compute a total, compare it to a limit, and justify the verdict in writing -- the full demand of the standard.

steps.rationale: Establish the substitute-compute-compare loop on friendly whole numbers. The standard's verb is 'use substitution to determine' -- before decimals or inequalities enter, the loop itself must be the student's default move instead of grabbing a number that looks right.

Run the same loop where estimation fails. The spec's difficult band uses only decimals, so 'which value makes the equation true' now requires exact computation -- close is not equal, and only substitution settles it.

Flip the frame: one fixed value, many equations. The value becomes a hypothesis tested in every equation on the list -- the first place the standard demands checking ALL candidates, not stopping at the first success.

Extend the true/false test from = to inequality symbols, the standard's second object. Each value in the table is judged independently, and at the boundary value the strict-versus-inclusive distinction does all the work.

One number, many inequalities. Truth is decided by substituting and reading the direction of the symbol -- not by how close the numbers look -- which is exactly the discrimination the standard's 'determine whether a given number makes it true' demands.

The standard's 'values from a specified set' lands here: a set contains only solutions when EVERY member passes. One failure disqualifies the set -- the quantifier 'only' is the new idea, layered on a loop the student already owns.

The above-proficiency demand: a real-world inequality with two variables. Students substitute a whole combination, compute the total, compare it to the limit, and write the justification -- demonstrating, not just finding, which values make the statement true.
